questions.title: SECTION A: ESSAY — Choose ONE essay topic from prompts 1.1–1.6.3 (400–450 words)

subQuestions.questionText:
NARRATIVE / REFLECTIVE

"There was a moment when I realised that silence can be louder than any word ever spoken."

Your essay may be personal, imaginative, or both. Focus on creating a meaningful moment or turning point.

[Write 400–450 words. Indicate the question number and the title of your essay. Do NOT count the title as part of your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
TOPIC-SPECIFIC LEVEL 4 INDICATORS:
• Establish a moment of meaningful silence — between people, within a memory, or in a broader social context.
• Use sensory detail to convey the weight of silence (what is NOT said, heard, or acknowledged).
• Create emotional resonance — the silence should mean something: loss, fear, defiance, unspoken love.
• Build toward a realisation or shift in understanding.

MEDIUM: Describes a silent moment without developing its emotional or thematic meaning.
LOW: Treats silence literally (e.g. a quiet classroom) with no emotional depth.

ESSAY MARKING RUBRIC (applies to all essay questions 1.1–1.6.3):

CONTENT & RELEVANCE (30 marks):
• LEVEL 4 (Excellent): Fully relevant; original insight; controlled central idea; powerful imagery/argument.
• LEVEL 3 (Good): Mostly relevant; clear ideas; consistently on topic; some depth.
• LEVEL 2 (Adequate): Generally relevant; ideas underdeveloped; limited insight.
• LEVEL 1 (Weak): Off-topic or superficial; ideas unclear.

LANGUAGE & STYLE (10 marks):
• LEVEL 4 (Excellent): Sophisticated vocabulary; varied sentences; consistent appropriate tone; fluent throughout.
• LEVEL 3 (Good): Good vocabulary; mostly varied; generally fluent; minor errors.
• LEVEL 2 (Adequate): Limited vocabulary; repetitive; errors impede flow.
• LEVEL 1 (Weak): Poor vocabulary; serious errors; inconsistent tone.

STRUCTURE & FORMAT (10 marks):
• LEVEL 4 (Excellent): Clear intro-body-conclusion; logical flow; correct paragraphing; title present; word count met.
• LEVEL 3 (Good): Structure visible; mostly logical; paragraphing adequate.
• LEVEL 2 (Adequate): Some structure; weak intro or conclusion; inconsistent paragraphing.
• LEVEL 1 (Weak): No clear structure; no paragraphing; no title.

[IMPORTANT: An off-topic essay cannot score more than 20/50 regardless of language quality. Reward authentic voice, original thought, and controlled craft. Do not penalise minor word-count overruns. Deduct 3 marks from Content only if substantially over 500 words.]

subQuestions.questionText:
ARGUMENTATIVE / DISCURSIVE

"South African young people are not failing their communities — their communities are failing them."

Present a clear argument, supported by evidence and reasoning. Acknowledge the opposing view.

[Write 400–450 words. Indicate the question number and the title of your essay. Do NOT count the title as part of your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
TOPIC-SPECIFIC LEVEL 4 INDICATORS:
• State a clear position in the introduction — do not merely restate the topic.
• Present at least TWO substantiated arguments (youth activism, innovation, civic engagement, academic achievement).
• Acknowledge the counter-position — some youth do disengage; structural challenges are real.
• Use specific examples — real or plausible — to anchor the argument.

MEDIUM: Clear opinion but limited development; limited counter-argument.
LOW: Opinion only; no evidence; descriptive rather than argumentative.

NARRATIVE / DESCRIPTIVE

"The last door in that house had been locked for eleven years."

Focus on creating a powerful sense of place, character, or moment. Your essay need not resolve its central tension.

[Write 400–450 words. Indicate the question number and the title of your essay. Do NOT count the title as part of your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
TOPIC-SPECIFIC LEVEL 4 INDICATORS:
• Create a strong sense of setting — the house should feel real, specific, atmospheric.
• Establish narrative tension around the locked door — what does it represent?
• Use figurative language purposefully: door as symbol of secrets, grief, shame.
• The essay need NOT resolve the tension — controlled ambiguity is rewarded.

MEDIUM: Describes the house but has no narrative tension or character development.
LOW: Lists events without creating atmosphere or character.

"Leaders who tell the truth are a greater threat to corrupt systems than any army."

[Write 400–450 words. Indicate the question number and the title of your essay. Do NOT count the title as part of your word count.]

subQuestions.questionText:
PICTURE PROMPT — Picture 1: 'The Unread Message'

Study Picture 1 in the question paper. The image shows a smartphone with a cracked screen displaying several unread messages from family members ('Mom', 'Thandi', 'Dad') with concerned text such as 'Are you okay? I haven't heard from you' and 'Please just answer me'. A hand reaches toward (or away from) the phone in a darkened space.

Write an essay of 400–450 words inspired by this picture. Your response may be narrative, descriptive, reflective, or argumentative. Give your essay a title.
subQuestions.memoText:
TOPIC-SPECIFIC LEVEL 4 INDICATORS:
• Use the phone, cracked screen, notifications, reaching hand as symbolic springboards.
• Write about loneliness, disconnection, urgency, love, or loss — all are valid.
• Avoid merely describing the picture — the image must LAUNCH the essay.

MEDIUM: Describes the picture accurately but develops no personal or thematic response.
LOW: Writes about technology in general with no real link to the image.

[Picture essays must show clear connection to the image — no visual relationship = max Level 2 Content.]

PICTURE PROMPT — Picture 2: 'The Empty Chair'

Study Picture 2 in the question paper. The image shows a warmly lit family dinner table set for a meal. A starlit window and an 'In Memoriam' photograph frame the scene. There is a single empty chair at the table, with a candle glowing nearby.

Write an essay of 400–450 words inspired by this picture. Your response may be narrative, descriptive, reflective, or argumentative. Give your essay a title.
subQuestions.memoText:
TOPIC-SPECIFIC LEVEL 4 INDICATORS:

questions.title: SECTION B: TRANSACTIONAL — Question 2: Formal Speech (Choose TWO tasks from Q2–Q7)

subQuestions.questionText:
FORMAL SPEECH (180–200 words)

The Student Representative Council (SRC) at your school has asked you to deliver a speech at a Youth Day assembly on 16 June. The theme for the event is: 'Our voices matter: the responsibility of young South Africans to shape their own future.'

Your speech should:
• open with an appropriate greeting and salutation to the audience
• clearly address the theme of youth responsibility and agency
• use persuasive and motivational language suited to a school audience
• end with a memorable closing statement or call to action

[Your speech must be 180–200 words. Do NOT count the heading/title in your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
• Formal greeting naming occasion and key people.
• Body addressing theme with clear paragraphs.
• Rhetorical devices: repetition, direct address, rhetorical questions.
• Motivational, inspiring tone — formal but energetic.
• Memorable closing or call to action.

LEVEL 4 CONTENT INDICATORS:
• Directly addresses theme: youth responsibility and agency.
• Specific examples of youth agency (protests, community projects, civic engagement).
• Clear structure: problem → solution → call to action.
• South African context (Youth Day, June 16) adds authenticity.
• Memorable, specific closing line — not generic.

MODEL ANSWER:
"Good morning, Principal Dlamini, Deputy Principal, teachers, and fellow learners.
Today — the 16th of June — we do not just observe a holiday. We honour a debt. In 1976, learners our age took to the streets of Soweto not knowing they would change the course of a nation. They had no social media, no platform, no guarantee of safety. They had only their voices — and they chose to use them.
Fifty years later, what is our excuse?
Too often I hear young people say: 'What can I do? I am just one person.' But Hector Pieterson was just one person. Malala Yousafzai was just one person. Our communities are not waiting for armies — they are waiting for us.
Our voices matter when we refuse to normalise corruption. Our voices matter when we speak up for a learner who is struggling. Our voices matter when we vote, volunteer, mentor, and lead — not because we are told to, but because we understand that no one else is coming.
South Africa's future belongs to the people in this hall. Let us be worthy of those who paid for it.
Thank you."

TRANSACTIONAL MARKING RUBRIC (applies to ALL tasks Q2–Q7):

CONTENT & TASK (12 marks):
• LEVEL 4 (Excellent): All task requirements met; rich detail; purpose fully achieved.
• LEVEL 3 (Good): Most requirements met; purpose clear; minor omissions.
• LEVEL 2 (Adequate): Some requirements met; purpose partially achieved.
• LEVEL 1 (Weak): Few requirements met; purpose unclear.

LANGUAGE & STYLE (7 marks):
• LEVEL 4 (Excellent): Sophisticated; controlled tone; word choice suits audience perfectly.
• LEVEL 3 (Good): Good control; appropriate tone; minor errors.
• LEVEL 2 (Adequate): Adequate; some tone issues; errors present.
• LEVEL 1 (Weak): Poor control; inappropriate tone; serious errors.

FORMAT & CONVENTIONS (6 marks):
• LEVEL 4 (Excellent): Correct format throughout; all conventions observed; word count appropriate.
• LEVEL 3 (Good): Mostly correct format; minor lapses.
• LEVEL 2 (Adequate): Some format elements present; significant lapses.
• LEVEL 1 (Weak): Wrong or absent format.

[FORMAT IS NON-NEGOTIABLE: A speech without greeting — max 2/6 for Format if substantially wrong. WORD COUNT: Penalise under 160 or over 220 by deducting 2 marks from Content. TONE: A speech that sounds like an essay loses Style marks.]

questions.title: SECTION B: TRANSACTIONAL — Question 3: Formal E-mail (Choose TWO tasks from Q2–Q7)

subQuestions.questionText:
FORMAL E-MAIL (180–200 words)

You are a Grade 12 learner at Sunrise High School. Your school recently introduced a 'no-phone policy' during all school hours. While you understand the intention, you believe it needs to make provision for emergency contact between learners and their parents. Write a formal e-mail to the School Principal, Mr D. Nkosi, to raise your concerns and suggest a practical alternative.

Your e-mail should:
• use correct e-mail format (To, From, Subject, salutation, body, closing)
• acknowledge the intention behind the policy before raising concerns
• suggest ONE clear, practical alternative
• maintain a formal and respectful tone throughout

[Your e-mail must be 180–200 words. Do NOT count the heading/title in your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
• To: Mr D. Nkosi (Principal) — e-mail address optional.
• From: Candidate's name.
• Subject: Clear, relevant subject line.
• Salutation: 'Dear Mr Nkosi' (NOT 'Hi' or 'Hello').
• Body: introduction + concern + proposal + closing.
• Sign-off: 'Yours sincerely,' + name.

LEVEL 4 CONTENT INDICATORS:
• Acknowledges purpose/benefits of no-phone policy before raising concern.
• States concern clearly: emergency communication between learners and parents.
• Proposes ONE specific, practical alternative.
• Formal, respectful tone throughout — never demanding.
• Logically structured: opening courtesy → acknowledgement → concern → proposal → closing.

MODEL ANSWER:
"To: d.nkosi@sunrisehigh.edu.za
From: lerato.mokoena@sunrisehigh.edu.za
Subject: Proposed Amendment to the No-Phone Policy

Dear Mr Nkosi,

I write on behalf of several Grade 12 learners to respectfully raise a concern regarding the recently implemented no-phone policy. I want to begin by acknowledging that the school's intention — to reduce distraction and improve focus — is entirely reasonable, and most learners support the spirit of the policy.

However, a number of us have experienced situations where a genuine emergency has arisen during the school day, and we have been unable to contact our parents or guardians promptly. This is a source of anxiety for both learners and their families.

I would respectfully propose that learners be permitted to contact parents in the case of a verified emergency through a supervised phone bay in the school office. This would maintain the integrity of the policy while ensuring urgent communication remains possible.

I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss this further at your convenience.

Yours sincerely,
Lerato Mokoena
Grade 12B"

• LEVEL 1 (Weak): Few requirements met; purpose unclear.

questions.title: SECTION B: TRANSACTIONAL — Question 4: Newspaper Article (Choose TWO tasks from Q2–Q7)

subQuestions.questionText:
NEWSPAPER ARTICLE (180–200 words)

A local community newspaper, The Ubuntu Voice, has asked learners to contribute articles on the following topic: 'The invisible crisis: how loneliness is quietly affecting South African youth.'

Your article should:
• include an eye-catching headline
• begin with a strong lead paragraph that establishes the topic
• use an informative and engaging tone suited to a general readership
• include at least ONE statistic, fact, or expert view (real or plausible)
• end with a concluding thought or call to awareness

[Your article must be 180–200 words. Do NOT count the headline in your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
• Headline: bold, concise, attention-grabbing — not a full sentence.
• Lead paragraph: answers who/what/where/why in 2–3 sentences.
• Body: developed points in paragraph form — NOT bullet points.
• Third-person register unless quoting a named source.
• Formal-informative tone — not conversational.

LEVEL 4 CONTENT INDICATORS:
• Strong, specific headline (NOT just 'Loneliness in Youth').
• Lead establishes the issue as a genuine crisis, not just a trend.
• At least ONE statistic, expert view, or plausible research reference.
• Explains WHY this is a crisis (social media, post-COVID isolation, economic stress).
• Closing thought that goes beyond summary — appeal, question, or warning.

MODEL ANSWER:
"SILENT EPIDEMIC: THE LONELINESS CRISIS SOUTH AFRICA'S YOUTH CANNOT NAME
By Our Youth Correspondent

Millions of South African young people carry a condition that has no visible symptoms and no accepted diagnosis — yet mental health experts warn it may be one of the most significant threats to youth wellbeing in a generation. Its name is loneliness.

According to the South African Depression and Anxiety Group (SADAG), reported feelings of persistent loneliness among adolescents have increased by nearly 35% since 2020. The causes are layered: the disruption of schooling during the COVID-19 pandemic, rising youth unemployment, and the paradox of social media — a technology that promises connection while quietly deepening isolation.

'We are seeing young people who have hundreds of online followers and no one to call at midnight,' said Dr Amara Dube, a Johannesburg-based adolescent psychologist.

Unlike hunger or homelessness, loneliness does not announce itself on the streets. It lives behind locked bedroom doors and glowing phone screens. South Africa cannot afford to wait for it to become visible before it responds."

questions.title: SECTION B: TRANSACTIONAL — Question 5: Dialogue (Choose TWO tasks from Q2–Q7)

subQuestions.questionText:
DIALOGUE (180–200 words)

Two close friends, Sipho and Amara, have a serious conversation. Sipho has recently discovered that Amara — who is applying to university — has been lying to their parents about their results. Sipho must decide whether to confront Amara, keep the secret, or encourage Amara to come clean.

Your dialogue should:
• be a realistic conversation between two characters who know each other well
• show both characters' attitudes and feelings through what they say
• include a moment of tension or turning point
• use natural spoken language with appropriate punctuation

[Your dialogue must be 180–200 words. Use speaker labels (SIPHO: / AMARA:). Do NOT count labels in your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
• Speaker labels clearly presented (SIPHO: / AMARA:).
• Natural spoken language — contractions, interruptions acceptable.
• NOT a narrative essay with speech marks — the dialogue IS the piece.
• Stage directions optional: brief and purposeful if included.

LEVEL 4 CONTENT INDICATORS:
• Distinct voices: Sipho and Amara do not sound identical.
• Believable context established quickly — no lengthy exposition.
• Tension is present and escalates — this is a difficult conversation.
• A clear turning point: Sipho decides what to do.
• Emotional authenticity visible through what characters say and how they say it.

MODEL ANSWER:
"SIPHO: I saw your results. The real ones.
AMARA: [pause] Where did you—
SIPHO: It doesn't matter. Amara, you're telling your parents you got seventy-two percent for Maths. Your actual mark is forty-eight.
AMARA: I know.
SIPHO: That's it? You know?
AMARA: What do you want me to say? You know what happens if my dad finds out. He'll pull me out of the application process completely. He thinks I'm going to be a doctor.
SIPHO: So you're going to let him pay for a future built on a lie?
AMARA: [quietly] I'm going to fix it. I just need time.
SIPHO: You've been saying that since April. I love you like a sister. But I can't keep pretending I don't know. Either you tell them, or I will.
AMARA: You wouldn't.
SIPHO: [long silence] I don't want to. But I also can't watch you disappear into something that wasn't real from the beginning.
[Neither speaks. Outside, a car alarm starts, then stops.]"

questions.title: SECTION B: TRANSACTIONAL — Question 6: Letter to the Press (Choose TWO tasks from Q2–Q7)

subQuestions.questionText:
LETTER TO THE PRESS (180–200 words)

You recently read a newspaper column by a journalist who argued that social media is 'nothing more than a narcissism machine that makes young people stupid, lonely, and vain.' You strongly disagree with parts of this view, although you acknowledge some concerns are valid. Write a letter to the editor of the newspaper in response.

Your letter should:
• use correct formal letter format (your address, date, editor's address, salutation, body, closing)
• acknowledge what the columnist got right before presenting your disagreement
• argue your position clearly with at least ONE example
• maintain a formal, measured, and respectful tone

[Your letter must be 180–200 words. Do NOT count address blocks or the heading in your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
• Sender's address (top right or left).
• Date.
• Editor's address (The Editor, name of newspaper).
• Salutation: 'Dear Editor' or 'Dear Sir/Madam'.
• Body: 3–4 paragraphs (acknowledgement → counter → evidence → conclusion).
• Formal closing: 'Yours faithfully,' + name.

LEVEL 4 CONTENT INDICATORS:
• Opens by acknowledging what the columnist got right.
• Clearly identifies what the columnist got wrong (overgeneralisation).
• Presents a specific counter-example or counter-argument.
• Formal, measured tone throughout — not aggressive.
• Concludes with nuanced position: social media requires education, not condemnation.

MODEL ANSWER:
"14 Ndlovu Road
Umhlanga
4320
15 April 2026

The Editor
The Daily Voice
Cape Town

Dear Editor,

I write in response to the column published on 10 April, in which the author characterised social media as 'a narcissism machine that makes young people stupid, lonely, and vain.' While I appreciate that the columnist has identified genuine concerns, I believe this assessment is both overstated and unfair.

It is true that excessive social media use has been linked to anxiety and social comparison. On this point, the columnist is not wrong. However, the same platforms that can isolate have also enabled extraordinary civic movements. The #FeesMustFall campaign, which transformed South African higher education policy, was organised largely through social media by the very young people the columnist dismisses as vain.

The problem is not the technology itself, but the absence of digital literacy education in our schools. Rather than condemning a generation, we should invest in teaching them to use these tools wisely.

Yours faithfully,
T. Ntanzi
Grade 12 Learner, Durban"

questions.title: SECTION B: TRANSACTIONAL — Question 7: Obituary (Choose TWO tasks from Q2–Q7)

subQuestions.questionText:
OBITUARY (180–200 words)

Nomvula Sithole, a beloved science teacher at Thornvale High School in Durban, passed away suddenly last week at the age of 54. She was known for her passionate teaching, her mentorship of girls in STEM, her sense of humour, and her tireless advocacy for learners from disadvantaged backgrounds. She is survived by her husband, two adult children, and her school community.

Your obituary should:
• open by announcing her death respectfully
• outline her key achievements, qualities, and contributions
• include at least ONE personal or human detail that brings her to life
• use formal, respectful, and commemorative language throughout
• end with a sentence capturing her legacy or a final tribute

[Your obituary must be 180–200 words. Do NOT count the headline in your word count.]
subQuestions.memoText:
FORMAT REQUIREMENTS:
• Headline: name + short descriptor.
• Opening: announces death — name, role, age, when.
• Body: achievements, character, specific contributions.
• Personal detail: at least one human/specific anecdote.
• Survivors listed.
• Closing tribute: legacy statement.
• Third person throughout; formal, warm, commemorative tone.

LEVEL 4 CONTENT INDICATORS:
• Announces her death clearly and with dignity in opening.
• Captures her primary identity as passionate science educator and mentor.
• Includes specific advocacy for girls in STEM — not just 'good teacher'.
• At least ONE personal detail making her feel real.
• Closes with tribute capturing her legacy, not just her loss.

MODEL ANSWER:
"NOMVULA SITHOLE (1971–2026): SHE TAUGHT GIRLS TO REACH FOR THE STARS — AND MEANT IT LITERALLY

Nomvula Sithole, beloved science teacher at Thornvale High School in Durban, passed away suddenly on 8 April 2026 at the age of 54. Her death has left a void in her school community that cannot be filled.

Ms Sithole joined Thornvale in 1998 and spent twenty-eight years building one of the most respected science departments in the province. She was known above all for her refusal to accept that any learner — regardless of background — was incapable of understanding physics or chemistry. 'The only thing standing between you and this subject,' she reportedly told every new class, 'is the story you're telling yourself about it.'

Her Girls in STEM programme, launched in 2011, mentored over three hundred young women, twelve of whom have since pursued careers in medicine, engineering, and research. She raised funds for the programme from her own salary.

She is survived by her husband Bongani, her children Zola and Themba, and the hundreds of learners who will carry her lessons for the rest of their lives.

She was, simply, the teacher everyone deserved."
